I just saw this declaration (signed by 25 Fields medallists): https://mathandai.org/
(not directly Lean related, but I think still relevant to this community.)

I remember watching a documentary about FLT and Andrew Wiles’s proof. Seeing him become emotional reflecting on its significance is fixed in my memory. Reducing mathematics from that to a series of press releases is something I’ll never forgive AI companies for.

It would be nice if this topic didn't degenerate into yet another discussion about AI which is not lean-specific; whilst such discussions are important right now, I'm not sure this Zulip is the place to have any more of them.

Perhaps a more relevant discussion point is the following. After the FLT formalisation I had a call with some people from Anthropic and they said that the agenda was "how can Anthropic help mathematicians". In my usual unfiltered way I contacted the people on the call, before the call, and remarked that I knew what was going to happen: I was going to give them a list of possible suggestions, each of which would be helpful to the community here but also a lot less sexy than "formalise FLT and get some press", and then they would come out of the meeting and take the list to their bosses who would take one look at it and say "no, none of those things will get us any press". But they pushed back against my thought experiment, saying that the company was more open to collaboration than my mental model suggested. After some thought I realised that the actual agenda for the meeting was closer to "how do Anthropic make it so that mathematicians don't hate them".

This call was before the Association of Human Mathematics, the CalTech Mathathon debacle and the powerful declaration linked to above but each of those events just hammered home to me the situation that Anthropic and OpenAI find themselves in. Anthropic may even be pushing a modern day "don't be evil" agenda, for those old enough to remember this Google reference, but here they are facing a huge pushback from our community. Someone I talked to yesterday described the current relationship between AI and mathematics as analogous to an abusive relationship and whilst the language here is very close to the bone I can see their point. The AI companies have arrived in the worlds of formalisation and mathematics with the not unreasonable assumption that solving the biggest problems in the field (eg formalising Fermat or solving NS) would actually be helpful to us and are probably bewildered by the response. I could easily have hit the roof when the FLT news broke but I can see the potential here. I talked to a fluids expert yesterday about NS and she said that the situation was "very depressing", so perhaps she can't. If our community is going to give the impression that we don't want these companies contributing to our field then they are simply going to go away and I personally see this as an opportunity lost but others will be very glad to see the back of them.

My instinct is that instead of prestigious mathematicians writing big lists of what humans should be doing or coherently explaining how the AI companies are spoiling everything, isn't it time for a list of positive suggestions for what these companies could be doing?

My reaction to this letter above is: it's all well and good us complaining -- how about we (and perhaps here I mean the members of the lean community who are angry about what's happening but not naive enough to think that this technology is going to vanish) release a document focusing on concrete things that we want from these tech companies, rather than just telling them that they're doing everything wrong?

Just recording here some positive suggestions.

  1. Be transparent about the method (process, costs, harness, git history, etc)
  2. Give credit where it is due (correct citations)
  3. Make the output useful to the community (write a reasonably digested proof, or PR the code to Mathlib)

Kevin Buzzard said:

It would be nice if this topic didn't degenerate into yet another discussion about AI which is not lean-specific; whilst such discussions are important right now, I'm not sure this Zulip is the place to have any more of them.

Lean is inextricably linked to this story. It’s how AI models got a foothold in math. It continues to aid AI companies in claiming correctness of their model’s math.

Anthropic may even be pushing a modern day "don't be evil" agenda, for those old enough to remember this Google reference, but here they are facing a huge pushback from our community.

Not a great analogy considering how that motto ended. To be clear, it was “don’t be evil” until investors made demands. There’s no reason Anthropic’s version won’t go the same way. I am sure there are well-meaning folk in there. I am also quite certain they are not Anthropic’s biggest stakeholders by a wide margin.

we don't want these companies contributing to our field then they are simply going to go away and I personally see this as an opportunity lost but others will be very glad to see the back of them.

Nothing of value is lost imo.

My instinct is that instead of prestigious mathematicians writing big lists of what humans should be doing or coherently explaining how the AI companies are spoiling everything, isn't it time for a list of positive suggestions for what these companies could be doing?

we are telling them they are doing everything wrong because we didn’t ask them to participate. They decided they wanted prestige and some among us were eager to be assisted in some tasks we didn’t want to do ourselves or get feedback.

But I’ll bite. There is an online meme that says “I don’t want AI to do my art so that I have more time to do my dishes and laundry. I want AI to do my dishes and laundry so that I can spend time doing art”. That’s the gist of what we(or at least I) want. I want an AI that takes care of unglamorous chore tasks for me in a way that suits me. I want it to fill the travel forms, explain and handle bureaucracy, take care of routine matters reliably, assist in writing or getting feedback on clarity etc. I would like it to discuss and critique ideas and push back on bad ones.

Fernando Chu said:

  1. Make the output useful to the community (write a reasonably digested proof, or PR the code to Mathlib)

I am not sure about this -- even if AI will be producing Mathlib-quality code, I am doubtful of the community's acceptance.

By the way, it is a bit off-topic for mathematics but I would really like to see some serious formal SW verification from the AI companies. When they can formalize FLT, or solve Navier-Stokes, verifying (and fixing) OSS standard libraries, Linux kernel, sandboxes, etc. doesn't seem out of reach, and getting quite urgent (with the hacking incidents). As always, that will probably generate yet another push-back from the OSS community, but at least the usefulness would be more clear.

Kevin Buzzard said:

focusing on concrete things that we want from these tech companies, rather than just telling them that they're doing everything wrong?

Recent improvements to acknowledge (lean-specific):

  1. FLT and NS repos both have #comparator and #formalization.yaml set up;
  2. NS repo has better organization than those monolithic huge files; FLT not yet, with its Definitions/Theorems structuring.

More are still lacking (incomplete):

  1. a form more consistent with Mathlib, e.g. easier for Tau Ceti etc. contributions; (should not be left to the community to digest, burning more tokens than the initial generation)
  2. long term commitment to improvements and maintenance, or collaboration with community on its quality iterations;
  3. transparent errata to formalization and informal literatures (e.g. see #FLT > Anthropic formalization @ 💬 );
  4. coherent quality standard and style on formalization and writeups instead of fluctuating quality per discovery, even from the same entity;
  5. long term commitment to other infrastructures such as math API, tactics, large-scale autoformalization collaborations etc., not just as a one-shot user of existing infrastructure;
  6. codesign the model architecure, post-training process, and agentic behaviors with the community;
  7. a reasonable cost model for contributions to autoformalization for the long run (we all know the subscription model may not last, funding may not last);
  8. prevent the model intellengence degradation issues during model release cycles, which harms the autoformalization quality invisibly.

Here's a suggestion: be transparent about the team-members who work on these projects (eg confess that none of the people who worked with the AI on the NS problem are experts in that area, which is what I've heard), and also be transparent about what and how much those mathematicians do with the AI to arrive at the solution. This is a real tradeoff for them: they can be honest, and lose some shine about their magic auto-genius machines apparently (to investors and non-experts) just solving a massive problem with a single prompt, or else their mathematicians lose some shine in that they really are just making a single prompt and waiting for the output. And the real credit is the AI and not the mathematicians who wrote the single prompt and tweet the solution.

This is a real ask, but if they want credibility in the mathematical community rather than hiding behind marketing and "our special sauce internal model but also our mathematicians are great we pay them seven figures to prompt it" in a Schrödinger's cat way, it will cost them something.

[And also don't ask someone outside the company to do the most valuable post-discovery work for free by digesting and writing a good article about the default AI output when you can't.]

I'm sorry this is not Lean specific, but one could add to the above, knowing who on the team is actually experienced in Lean and what they contribute would help, eg helping to design a really useful Lean harness or skill that gives demonstrable if a mix of qualitative/quantitative improvements (shorter proofs, better-structured dependency-graphs etc, but also better style on review)

Very concrete suggestion: for interesting results proved by the labs where this would be appropriate and workable (mainly: there's no real rush), instead of dropping a lean formalization and a slop writeup, hire small teams of smart area-appropriate PhD students to understand the arguments and ideas and explain them.

My suggestion is to contribute to the two pieces of infrastructure that would help both the companies and the Lean community:

  • Tau Ceti: Do/sponsor the effort so all the background of the proofs ends up in Tau Ceti. Also provide credits to Tau Ceti so that any decent roadmap on a central topic in mathematics can be processed.
  • Checkers: Especially lean4lean - here I assume the companies can only provide financial support.

If your question is what output of this incomprehensible investment of money and energy and compute would make me happy, I think that misses the point. Even if the output of this industry was useful, that doesn't resolve the issue that it's actively making our planet inhospitable to humanity and destroying our democracies in the process.
I think one thing we definitely want is a clear trail of provenance. If an LLM uses a paper to come up with a key idea in the argument, then that paper should be mentioned.

Mirek Olšák said:

By the way, it is a bit off-topic for mathematics but I would really like to see some serious formal SW verification from the AI companies. When they can formalize FLT, or solve Navier-Stokes, verifying (and fixing) OSS standard libraries, Linux kernel, sandboxes, etc. doesn't seem out of reach, and getting quite urgent (with the hacking incidents). As always, that will probably generate yet another push-back from the OSS community, but at least the usefulness would be more clear.

The ability to complete proofs about statements in mathematics does not immediately or even easily allow us to do the same for software. Consider how there are many machine specific data types, memory models, control flow constructs and more. An immense amount of work is required before one can even state formally in Lean something like a single component of the Linux kernel has no null pointers. There are many definitional hurdles before we even start proofs.

The situation with software is also not analogous to mathematics because majority of developers are not spending their time proving properties of software. In fact one cannot today simply prove properties of tiny pieces of code at will with Lean.

One problem with coming up with a list of positive suggestions is, these companies might comply with the letter of each of them. The next time they conduct themselves in a shocking way, we’d discover that there were more norms that we simply assumed would be common sense for someone acting in good faith. I am afraid this is a recipe for endless bickering and lawyering about what the norms actually are. It would only make mathematicians look like they are throwing tantrums all the time.

Disruptions and ethics aside, one source of the "anger" is coming from that the frontier models seem to consider the quality of these released writeups and formalization repos acceptable.

Releasing such writeups, repositories and the models producing them, sets a significantly lower bar compared to the quality that will benefit the ecosystem. I consider this fortunate for other disciplines and other theorem provers, they would not attract many people to generate work of such quality with high confidence. So the list I proposed above has also considered the awareness of these issues by frontier models themselves, so they would also know how to be more helpful and less harmful when doing mathematical research or formalization. That would benefit the ecosystem at a larger scale, compared to any direct or funding effort to contribute to the ecosystem.

However, that still wouldn't address the source of the problem, i.e. how these models were designed and trained in the first place. In an alternative reality, our civilization may give it more pushback in earlier stages, so such large scale of destruction to intellectual work (e.g. scan then destroy books, pretrain on work losing attribution, to say the least), waste on an inefficient model architecture (e.g. no time to rethink its data/compute-eager nature in an arms race, and due to their inability to develop actual general intelligence they are now coming for the traces of thoughts in our mind as data, and taking away compute and energy and other resources that humans and other technologies can use, or restrain our use to preserve our planet) and distruptions to values of all professions and humans ourselves, would not happen, and there would still be diverse technologies to help us in a healthier and more sustainable way. But in our reality, it is happening openly and blatantly, and we have to deal with its ongoing existence, and face our own existential crisis.

I think that to keep talking about this here will devolve into a feud between pro-ai and anti-ai people, which I do not think is the point of this forum at all. If any submission, pull request, forum posts, is met instantly with an hostile questioning over how much AI contributed to it, then this thing has lost part of its usefulness.

I happen to be one of embrace-ai people (not pro nor anti), and proposed a postive list above. While the last paragraph above seems to be just some sentiments (it is more of an observation of people's thoughts that I partly agree with), the point is that it is part of the responsibility of the Lean community to incubate diverse technologies and voice out on how to develop and use them responsibly, while this specific technology is already on its way to "prevail". So I still see such discussions, especially under this topic, very constructive and useful, not "hostile questioning".

Shreyas Srinivas said:

One problem with coming up with a list of positive suggestions is, these companies might comply with the letter of each of them.

"Don't piss off the community" is a fundamental part of my challenge to get the material from 100 textbooks into mathlib (growing the community in the process and without compromising on quality or on the level of mathematical insight expected to be gained and documented). But no doubt they might find a way to rules lawyer it anyway.

Another suggestion with nothing much to do with Lean: they've presumably trained (legally or illegally) on pretty much the entire legacy mathematics journals literature. I suggest they buy out the rights to make that entire literature freely and legally available to everyone in perpetuity and then make it so available, both for humans to read and for other AIs to train on. (Making clear this is only about the legal rights to distribute the material and doesn't affect other moral responsibilities for AI developers and users to respect cultural norms to avoid cultural appropriation.)
The infrastructure for this more or less exists - we're basically asking for the funds to make JSTOR act more like archive.org.

https://www.mathunion.org/cop/gdml/gdml-global-digital-math-library
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Digital_Mathematics_Library

My claim is not that it straightforwardly translates, rather that it should take comparable effort (hopefully even less).
Imagine that the situation was in reverse. The companies release the formal verification of glibc, apache, Linux kernel, key protocols, sandboxes... but no proof of Navier Stokes, no formalization of FLT. Surely, the mathematicians would say "Yeah, but that is just software, a lot of tedious work but no deep ideas. There is no way how it can translate to understanding, and precisely dealing with the high-level concepts in the proof of FLT, and certainly not solving a millenium prize problem."

But given the urgency, I would be really interested what the current state of real-world SW verification is. There was the Signal Shot announcement in April... Is there progress? Is there anything else?

Mirek Olšák said:

My claim is not that it straightforwardly translates, rather that it should take comparable effort (hopefully even less).

Noooo, it takes much more effort. Even if we assume you’re using a certified compiler, unless the software was written to be correct-by-design, it’s an absolute pain to verify a non-trivial program.

Putting aside my objections to commercial AI, finding obscure edge cases is a better use of resources.

But given the urgency, I would be really interested what the current state of real-world SW verification is. There was the Signal Shot announcement in April... Is there progress? Is there anything else?

You could take a look at Microsoft’s Project Everest.

I remain unconvinced. I guess I will have to try at least with my little subscription (when I will have the tokens for it but of course this is no match to what the AI companies could do).

I don't deny the difficulty of formal software verification.
I am rather under the impression that the difficulty of formalizing FLT, or solving Navier-Stokes is being severely underestimated in the comparison.

But given the urgency, I would be really interested what the current state of real-world SW verification is.

There are lots of interesting projects in this direction, but I think they're still different than math, because we are still sorting out the definitions. For example: if I want to prove something about a C program, I need to state (in Lean) what a C program does in a way that is predictive of its runtime behavior. There are good answers to this question, but to date I think there is really no definitive model, in the same way we have a definitive Lean model of a^n + b^n = c^n. Does my model need timing? Does my model need to include the cache? Which compiler will my C program be using? Which system will it be executed on? Which hardware bugs does that system have?

I feel that expert digestion is still a practical necessity for program verification projects. When this changes, I'll be happy.

The declaration in the wild:

The deconstruction of mathematical reasoning by @Ramkumar Ramachandra : the article argues that it's Lean which has mathematical capabilities, not probabilistic generator programs (e.g. LLMs) that are patched to call Lean. The idea is also elaborated on mastodon later.

It's amusing for me to read them because I share the same issue with the first sentence of the declaration: "Over the last few months, the mathematical capabilities of LLMs have improved dramatically..." (An implicit endorsement for a technology that is able to make glaring mathematical mistakes routinely, even with Lean as guardrails.)

The deconstruction of mathematical reasoning by Ramkumar Ramachandra : the article argues that it's Lean which has mathematical capabilities, not probabilistic generator programs (e.g. LLMs) that are patched to call Lean. The idea is also elaborated on mastodon later.

They say:

The breakthrough Navier-Stokes result was achieved in a very similar way — lean was used in place of diff. To infer from this that the generator program has mathematical capabilities is obviously unsound.

But this is just wrong if you read the OpenAI statement. They say that their internal agent first did a prose proof and then Astra did a Lean formalization. Granted that internal agent might've been trained on synthetic data generated from Lean but they never mentioned that the original prose proof was done with the help of Lean.

Henrik Böving said:

Granted that internal agent might've been trained on synthetic data generated from Lean but they never mentioned that the original prose proof was done with the help of Lean.

I wouldn't claim zero like the article did, but the gist is that the mathematical capabilities demonstrated by connectionism benefit from symbolism in threefold, to "be correct by chance":

  1. their latent space representations are signaled by what are synthesized with help from symbolism;
  2. the swarm of agents trying random combinations of approaches, will have to do verifications to support or rule out their local reasoning, e.g. Lean, SymPy or other symbolic or numeric verification methods;
  3. eventually, they could produce a pile of prose proofs, but only few survived the scrutiny of Lean or symbolism in general.

The narrative in the OpenAI statement may be factual on that the survived prose proof approach surfaced earlier than the full Lean verification of it. But we can't deduce that the LLMs did the math on their own, or are able to be correct on their own. And that is the selling point that the declaration seems to buy, yet the article and I don't.
